rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Power is the rate of energy delivery: $P = W/t$, or instantaneously $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v$ — for a vehicle at uniform speed the engine force just balances resistance, so $P = F_{res}v$ (a 1000 kg car at 20 m/s against 500 N needs 10 kW — NEB 2024).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - P = W/t; P = Fv cos θ - 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; 1 hp ≈ 746 W - Lifting: t = mgh/P; climbing: P = mgh/t

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: P=F⃗·v⃗ uses instantaneous force and velocity; it applies even when force changes with time.  ·  For efficiency, state whether the requested power is input or useful output.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Do not use P=Fv unless force and velocity are parallel or include cosθ.  ·  Motor output is not the net power on a constant-speed vehicle.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: **kW vs kWh:** kilowatt is power (rate); kilowatt-hour is energy (power × time) — the bill charges for kWh.  ·  **Engine power at uniform speed:** F = resistance (a = 0), so P = F_resistance × v — not ma × v.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: A 1200 kg car moves at 20 m s⁻¹ against 600 N drag. Find power to maintain speed.  ·  Why does centripetal force do zero work in uniform circular motion?

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): A pump lifts 200 kg of water per minute to a height of 10 m. Calculate the power of the pump (g = 10 m/s²).** — Work per minute = mgh = 200 × 10 × 10 = 20,000 J; P = 20,000/60 ≈ 333 W (NEB 2024).

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Power prices time, not effort:** the same mgh costs more power when delivered faster.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: P = W/t = Fv cos θ; watt = J/s.  ·  1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J (NEB 2024).  ·  Motor lifting: t = mgh/P. Human climbing: P = mgh/t. Vehicle: P = F_resistance × v.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: A human at sustained hard work delivers 100–300 W — roughly the power of a bright old-style light bulb.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Rate of Energy Delivery Two cranes can lift the same car, but only the powerful one lifts it quickly. Power measures work per unit time — the billing unit of the electricity grid (the kilowatt-hour) and the performance metric of engines, pumps and athletes.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts | Quantity | Definition | Formula | Unit | |---|---|---|---| | **Power** | Work done per unit time | $P = W/t$ | watt (W) = J/s | | **Instantaneous power** | Rate at an instant | $P = \vec F\cdot\vec v = Fv\cos\theta$ | W | | **Kilowatt-hour** | Commercial energy unit: energy delivered by 1 kW for 1 hour | $1\,\text{kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6$ J | — |…  ·  ## 3. Conceptual Relationships - **To Topic 16:** power is work's time derivative — same energy, different delivery rate. - **To Topic 18:** $P = Fv$ comes from differentiating the work–energy theorem: $P = dW/dt = F\,ds/dt$. - **To electrical circuits (Unit 25):** $P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$ — the same watt in electrical dress.…
